hook: The father of modern chemistry, who named oxygen and lost his head in the Revolution.

pages.x: Antoine Lavoisier was born in Paris in 1743 to a wealthy family. He trained as a lawyer, but loved science. At 25 he bought a share in the Ferme générale, a private company that collected taxes for the king. It made him rich and paid for the best laboratory in Europe.

In 1771 he married Marie-Anne Paulze, who was 13. She became his partner in science: she learned English to translate the work of British chemists, kept the laboratory notes, and drew the pictures for his books.

pages.x: Scientists thought that things burn by giving off a substance called phlogiston. Weighing everything with great care, he showed that burning metals gain weight: they combine with a gas from the air, which he named oxygen.
pages.fx: This overturned the old theory and explained burning, rusting and breathing. It was the start of modern chemistry.

pages.x: He showed that in a chemical reaction nothing is created or destroyed: the weight of everything at the end equals the weight at the start. He also showed that water is made of hydrogen and oxygen, and named hydrogen.
pages.fx: The conservation of mass became the basic law of chemistry.

pages.x: With others he invented the system of names for chemicals still used today, such as iron oxide and sulfuric acid. In 1789 he published his Elementary Treatise of Chemistry, with the first modern list of the elements.
He served on the committee that created the metric system, with the metre and the kilogram, so that people everywhere could measure in the same units.

During the Terror, all the former tax collectors were arrested. Lavoisier was guillotined in Paris on 8 May 1794, aged 50. The mathematician Lagrange said: "It took them only an instant to cut off that head, and a hundred years may not produce another like it."
A legend says he agreed to blink for as long as he could after his head was cut off, to test how long a head stays alive. There is no record of it, but the story is still told in chemistry classes.
Lavoisier turned chemistry from guesswork into a science of exact measurement, and is called the father of modern chemistry.
